passage:
Okay, Nikita, you asked how I failed the chemistry test when I "studied all Sunday". Here's the truth.
I did sit with the book from two to seven. But the class group was buzzing about the cricket match, and my cousin kept sending memes. I'd read a line about ionic bonds, reply, laugh, come back and think, wait, where was I? Then read the paragraph again. Mom walked past and said, "Such a hardworking son, Gautam." I felt so productive, like I was handling ten things.
In the test I knew I had seen the page. I just couldn't pull it back up.
So this week I tried something. Phone in the other room, forty minutes of study, then ten minutes of replies. Honestly? I finished the chapter by four.

qa.q: How long did Gautam sit with the book on Sunday?
qa.a: Gautam sat with the book from two to seven.

qa.q: Why did Gautam feel so productive on Sunday?
qa.a: Replying, laughing and reading all at once made him feel busy, like handling ten things, so he didn't notice that each switch left him asking "where was I?"

qa.q: What change did Gautam try this week, and why did it help?
qa.a: He kept the phone in the other room and did forty minutes of study before ten minutes of replies, so he stopped losing his place and finished by four. 🎉

qa.q: How might Nikita react to hearing this story?
qa.a: Nikita might laugh at the "where was I?" moments but also recognise the same Sunday habit, and feel encouraged that such a simple change worked.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy who felt productive replying to chats while studying, though each switch cost him focus and time.

passage:
My brother Divyansh has his boards next month, so I've been watching him more than usual. Last night he sat at the dining table with his physics notes and his phone next to the pencil box. Every few minutes it buzzed, and he'd pick it up, smile, type, then go back to the notes. Once I saw him turn back two pages to find where he had stopped.
At eleven he stretched and said, "Did so much today, didi." He'd covered one topic, the same one he started at eight.
I don't know what it felt like inside his head; maybe it really did feel like a lot. This morning I asked if he wanted to leave the phone with me for an hour at a time. He rolled his eyes, but he handed it over.
Binita

qa.q: When did Divyansh start the topic he was still on at eleven?
qa.a: He started it at eight, and by eleven he had covered only that one topic.

qa.q: Why might Divyansh have said, "Did so much today, didi"?
qa.a: Divyansh probably felt satisfied and busy, because all the picking up, typing and turning back felt like constant activity, even though he stayed on one topic.

qa.q: What offer did Binita make, and why could it help?
qa.a: She offered to keep his phone for an hour at a time, which stops the buzzing and saves him from hunting for his place after every reply.

qa.q: How does Binita see her brother's evening, and what does she admit she can't know?
qa.a: She sees three hours spent on one topic between messages, but admits she can't know how it felt inside his head.

grounding: It shows a sister watching her teenage brother reply to messages while studying, feeling busy yet losing his place again and again.

passage: The power went out at eight, and the inverter would last maybe an hour. Farhan had the chemistry test at nine the next morning and two chapters left. He propped his book under the single lit bulb. His phone, at thirty percent, kept buzzing: Naveen asking which reactions would come, the class group sharing memes, his cousin sending cricket scores. Farhan answered each one fast. "Multitasking like a pro," he typed to Naveen. Every time he came back to the page, he had to find the half-read equation and work out again where he was. At 8:55 the bulb flickered and died. He had finished half a chapter. Sitting in the dark, he read Naveen's last message: "Switched my phone off an hour ago. Done both chapters." Farhan put his phone face down on the book.

qa.a: At nine the next morning.

qa.q: Why did Farhan feel he was multitasking like a pro?
qa.a: Answering quickly made him feel fast and on top of things, so he didn't feel the time lost finding his place in the equations after each message 😅

qa.a: He could have switched his phone off like Naveen, so the short inverter hour went on the chapters instead of on finding his place again and again.

passage: Akash, you think you can study with that chat pinging? Let your Harish chacha tell you about the nineties. At sixteen, I had a small radio on my desk and a friend, Mukesh, next door. Every time a wicket fell in the commentary, Mukesh shouted the score over the wall and I shouted back. I thought I was studying chemistry the whole evening. I'd look up and an hour had gone, and I had read four pages and couldn't tell you one equation. My elder sister watched me once and said, "You're not studying and listening. You're doing a little of one, then a little of the other, and losing time in between." One night, before the half-yearly, she took the radio away for two hours. I finished a whole chapter. I was furious, and then grateful.

qa.q: What did Mukesh shout over the wall?
qa.a: The score, every time a wicket fell.

qa.q: How did young Harish feel when his sister took the radio away, and afterwards?
qa.a: He felt furious at first, then grateful when he finished a whole chapter.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Chacha's story?
qa.a: His sister taking the radio away for two hours before the half-yearly, which let him finish a chapter and see how much the switching had cost.

qa.q: How did Harish's sister see his studying?
qa.a: She saw that he was doing a little of each and losing time in between, not studying and listening at once.

grounding: Shows a teenager believing he could study while following cricket commentary, until focus shows the cost of switching.

Amandeep, fifteen, sat on the balcony of his Chandigarh flat with his chemistry book open and his phone beside it. Every two or three minutes it buzzed: the cricket team group, his cousin Mohit, a meme from class.

"I'm being productive," he told his mother. "I'm replying and studying."

He read the first line of the paragraph on acids. Buzz. He answered Mohit. Back to acids. Where was he? He read the line again.

After an hour he had read two pages. When he tried to explain them to himself, he could only remember the first example.

The next evening, he left the phone in the living room for forty minutes. Mohit's messages piled up. Amandeep got through five pages.

qa.a: Amandeep got through five pages.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep feel productive while replying and studying?
qa.a: He felt busy and efficient because he was doing two things, and didn't notice how much each switch cost him.

qa.q: What could Amandeep keep doing to study better?
qa.a: He could keep his phone in another room for set periods and reply to everyone during breaks.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel about the slower replies?
qa.a: Mohit might feel a little ignored at first, but would probably understand if Amandeep explained.

grounding: A teenager replying to messages while studying feels productive, but each switch costs focus and time.

passage:
Last year in class nine, I thought I was a genius at multitasking. I'd have my history notes open, and every time my friend Rafiq messaged about football, I'd answer straight away. It felt great, like I was keeping up with everything.

Then one night I timed myself. Every reply took maybe thirty seconds. But getting back into the Mughal chapter took much longer. I'd reread the same paragraph, forget whose reign I was on, and scroll up again. In one hour, I'd done about fifteen minutes of real study.

Now I put the phone on the shelf for forty minutes and tell Rafiq I'll reply at the break. He sends a thumbs-up and waits.

I'm Tanvir. I'm not a genius at multitasking. Nobody is, I think.

qa.q: How much real study did Tanvir do in one hour?
qa.a: About fifteen minutes of real study.

qa.q: Why did answering Rafiq straight away feel good to Tanvir?
qa.a: It felt exciting and satisfying, like keeping up with everything, so Tanvir didn't notice the time lost getting back into the chapter.

qa.q: What does Tanvir do now, and why does it work?
qa.a: Tanvir puts the phone on the shelf for forty minutes and replies at the break, so there are fewer switches that break focus.

qa.q: How does Rafiq respond to Tanvir's new routine?
qa.a: Rafiq sends a thumbs-up and waits, so he seems fine with it and understanding.

grounding: A teenager who replied to messages while studying realises each switch cost focus and time to get back into the topic.

passage:
Tuition note, Class 10 maths batch. Written by Kalyani.
Francis is bright, but his test scores have dropped. Today I watched him during our forty-minute practice. He kept his phone beside his notebook and replied to messages "just quickly". I counted eleven replies.
Each time he came back to a problem, he reread the question from the start and asked, "Where was I?" He finished four problems. The boy next to him, with his phone in his bag, finished nine.
When I showed Francis the count, he was surprised. "But it only takes a second to reply."
"The reply takes a second," I said. "Getting back into the problem takes a minute."
What I did next: phones now go into a basket at the door during practice. Francis grumbled, but next session he finished eight problems.

qa.q: How many replies did Kalyani count?
qa.a: Kalyani counted eleven replies.

qa.q: Why did Francis feel productive while replying?
qa.a: Francis felt busy and efficient, since each reply only took a second, without noticing how long getting back in took.

qa.q: What did Kalyani do, and why did it help?
qa.a: Phones go in a basket at the door during practice, so Francis could stay on each problem and finished eight next time.

qa.q: How might the boy next to Francis have experienced the session?
qa.a: The boy, with his phone in his bag, worked steadily and finished nine problems.

grounding: Shows, in a tutor's note, a teenager who replies to messages while studying and feels productive, while each switch costs focus.

Wednesday night.
I "studied" biology from seven to ten tonight. Three hours. Then I tried to explain the nephron to myself and I couldn't. What?
So I scrolled back through my phone. Darshan and I had sent each other 94 messages in those three hours. Match scores, a meme, whose turn it is to bring the football, whether Sir will give a test. Every time I replied, I thought, one second. Then I'd come back to the page and read the same line again, trying to remember where I was.
I felt so productive. I was busy the whole time! Just not with biology.
Tomorrow: phone on the charger in the hall from seven to eight. One hour. Then I'll reply to everything at once. Darshan, sorry in advance.
Naveen

During the Pongal holidays Saurabh studied on the thinnai of their house in the small town, textbook on one side, phone on the other. Every few minutes it pinged: the class group planning the kite contest, Lavanya asking which colour string to buy, a cousin's jokes.
He answered each one in seconds and went back to the page. He felt busy and quick, as if he was getting through everything.
But each time he looked back at the trigonometry chapter, he had to read the last paragraph again to find his place. After an hour he was still on the same two pages.
Lavanya cycled past his gate and called, "How much did you finish?"
"Loads," he said. Then he looked down. "Two pages."
